newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel drops request U.S. hand over Hamas leader.
newsitem.headline: Israel drops request U.S. hand over Hamas leader.

text.p: Israel on Thursday dropped a request that the United States hand over a Hamas leader, a decision security sources said was prompted by fear of a violent backlash.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said Israel had suspended an 18-month-old extradition request for Mousa Mohammed Abu Marzook, a political leader of the Islamic fundamentalist Hamas group, for reasons "relating to security and the prevention of terrorism".
Hamas had warned it would attack Israelis and would cast the United States as an enemy of "Islamic people everywhere" if the extradition went through.

"This is strong evidence that the American administration's accusations against Abu Marzook were false," said Ghazi Hamad, editor of the Hamas-affiliated Islamist newspaper al-Risala in the Palestinian-ruled Gaza Strip.
Security sources said Israel had feared the extradition would spark a wave of violence.

An Israeli official, speaking on condition he not be identified, said the extradition could damage efforts to fight Hamas and Islamic Jihad, two Palestinian groups behind suicide attacks that have killed scores of Israelis.

The official said these efforts to fight "terrorist organisations" also involved Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority. Arafat had himself asked Washington not to hand Abu Marzook to Israel. One scenario had Abu Marzook going to Jordan.
Abu Marzook, a longtime U.S. resident jailed in New York since his arrest in July 1995, had denied involvement in violence but stopped fighting his extradition in January.

Israel had alleged the U.S.-educated Gazan had a role in a number of fatal bombings, shootings and stabbings between 1990 and 1994 and, as head of the political arm, had raised money for and controlled the leadership of the military wing of Hamas.
The reversal by Netanyahu, a right-winger, contrasted sharply with the formal, 900-page extradition request that Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin's centre-left government submitted in October 1995.
When it sought Abu Marzook's extradition 18 months ago, Israel said he would face charges of murder, conspiracy and unspecified "other crimes".

Netanyahu, an author of books on counter-terrorism, came to power last May on a promise to protect Israelis from a wave of Islamist suicide attacks that killed 59 people in the run-up to the election.

But the Israeli official said: "The current request by the Israeli government does not represent any kind of precedent for any future cases and the Israeli government stressed this in its request to the U.S. administration."
Abu Marzook's lawyer argued in a New York court on Tuesday that his client should be freed, citing U.S. laws requiring the government to surrender him to Israel or release him no later than March 28.

Israel did not contend that Abu Marzook personally committed any of the violent acts, but charged he was criminally liable because of his high-level role in allegedly directing, controlling and financially supporting Hamas's activities.

He was arrested on July 25, 1995, at a New York airport as he flew to the United States after immigration officials found his name on its "watch list" of people with "known or suspected ties to terrorist activities."
Abu Marzook has a home and business in the U.S. state of Virginia, but U.S. and Israeli authorities charged he frequently travelled to the Middle East to promote violence and undermine peace efforts.
